claim: 93% of myelinated neurons, as determined by neurofilament heavy chain (NFH) labeling, express Scn1a transcripts.
source: RNAscope analysis of DRG sections from adult mice showed that 93% of myelinated neurons, as determined by neurofilament heavy chain (NFH) labeling, express Scn1a transcripts (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNAscope analysis data shown in Figure 1A with quantification in pie chart.

claim: 100% of genetically identified proprioceptors express Scn1a mRNA.
source: we next analyzed NaV1.1 expression in these cells using a ParvalbuminCre;Rosa26Ai14 reporter line (PvalbAi14) and found that 100% of genetically identified proprioceptors were positive for Scn1a message (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by RNAscope analysis using PvalbAi14 reporter mice shown in Figure 1B with quantification.

claim: 24% of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP)-expressing neurons express Scn1a mRNA.
source: This contrasted with low expression of Scn1a mRNA in both calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP)-expressing neurons, which represent peptidergic nociceptors, and non-peptidergic polymodal Mrgprd-expressing nociceptors (24 and 3%, respectively, Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by RNAscope analysis data shown in Figure 1C with quantification.

claim: 3% of non-peptidergic polymodal Mrgprd-expressing nociceptors express Scn1a mRNA.
source: This contrasted with low expression of Scn1a mRNA in both calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP)-expressing neurons, which represent peptidergic nociceptors, and non-peptidergic polymodal Mrgprd-expressing nociceptors (24 and 3%, respectively, Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by RNAscope analysis data shown in Figure 1D with quantification.

claim: 100% of genetically identified proprioceptors express Scn8a mRNA.
source: As with Scn1a, mRNA for Scn8a and Scn9a is also found in 100% of genetically identified proprioceptors (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by RNAscope analysis data shown in Figure 2A with quantification.

claim: 100% of genetically identified proprioceptors express Scn9a mRNA.
source: As with Scn1a, mRNA for Scn8a and Scn9a is also found in 100% of genetically identified proprioceptors (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by RNAscope analysis data shown in Figure 2B with quantification.

claim: The coefficient of variation for Scn1a transcript expression in proprioceptors is 75.6.
source: The CV for Scn1a transcript expression was calculated to be 75.6, whereas this value increased to 97.3 and 88.1 for Scn8a and Scn9a, respectively.
evidence: Calculated from integrated fluorescence density measurements of Scn1a expression.

claim: The coefficient of variation for Scn8a transcript expression in proprioceptors is 97.3.
source: The CV for Scn1a transcript expression was calculated to be 75.6, whereas this value increased to 97.3 and 88.1 for Scn8a and Scn9a, respectively.
evidence: Calculated from integrated fluorescence density measurements of Scn8a expression.

claim: The coefficient of variation for Scn9a transcript expression in proprioceptors is 88.1.
source: The CV for Scn1a transcript expression was calculated to be 75.6, whereas this value increased to 97.3 and 88.1 for Scn8a and Scn9a, respectively.
evidence: Calculated from integrated fluorescence density measurements of Scn9a expression.

claim: NaV1.1 has the most consistent level of expression across proprioceptors compared to NaV1.6 and NaV1.7.
source: This indicates that while all three isoforms are ubiquitously expressed in proprioceptors, the relative levels differ, with NaV1.1 having the most consistent level of expression across neurons analyzed.
evidence: Based on coefficient of variation analysis showing NaV1.1 has the lowest CV (75.6) compared to NaV1.6 (97.3) and NaV1.7 (88.1).

claim: The average integrated density of the NaV1.1 signal in proprioceptors is significantly higher than that of NaV1.6 and NaV1.7 (p<0.0001).
source: Furthermore, the average integrated density of the NaV1.1 signal for a given proprioceptive DRG neuron was significantly higher than the average integrated densities calculated for both NaV1.6 and NaV1.7 (Figure 2E, p<0.0001).
evidence: Supported by quantification of integrated density measurements shown in Figure 2E with statistical analysis.

claim: 44.8% of the proprioceptor whole-cell sodium current is sensitive to ICA 121431 (NaV1.1 antagonist).
source: We found that the ICA-sensitive component was 44.8% of INa.
evidence: Determined by serial pharmacological blockade experiments in proprioceptors shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: 14.5% of the proprioceptor whole-cell sodium current is sensitive to AH-TTX (NaV1.6 antagonist).
source: Conversely, 14.5 and 32.9% of INa was sensitive to AH-TTX and PF-05089771, respectively (Figure 2G).
evidence: Determined by serial pharmacological blockade experiments in proprioceptors shown in Figure 2G.

claim: 32.9% of the proprioceptor whole-cell sodium current is sensitive to PF-05089771 (NaV1.7 antagonist).
source: Conversely, 14.5 and 32.9% of INa was sensitive to AH-TTX and PF-05089771, respectively (Figure 2G).
evidence: Determined by serial pharmacological blockade experiments in proprioceptors shown in Figure 2G.

claim: 7.8% of the proprioceptor whole-cell sodium current remained unblocked following serial application of NaV antagonists.
source: On average, 7.8% of the current remained unblocked following serial application of these antagonists due to incomplete block by the drugs used.
evidence: Determined by serial pharmacological blockade experiments in proprioceptors.

claim: Proprioceptors do not express TTX-resistant NaVs.
source: Finally, we blocked NaV1.7 channels using the antagonist PF-05089771 (25 nM), followed by tetrodotoxin (TTX, 300 nM) to block any residual current, as proprioceptors do not express TTX-resistant NaVs.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the context of experimental design.

claim: The first detectable sodium current in proprioceptors appears at voltages near –50 mV when evoked from a holding potential of –90 mV.
source: The current–voltage relationship shows the first detectable current appeared at voltages near –50 mV and was maximal at voltages near –30 mV when evoked from a holding potential of –90 mV (Figure 3B).
evidence: Determined by voltage-clamp experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The sodium current in proprioceptors is maximal at voltages near –30 mV when evoked from a holding potential of –90 mV.
source: The current–voltage relationship shows the first detectable current appeared at voltages near –50 mV and was maximal at voltages near –30 mV when evoked from a holding potential of –90 mV (Figure 3B).
evidence: Determined by voltage-clamp experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The voltage for half-maximal activation of sodium channels in proprioceptors is –38.7 mV.
source: Voltage dependence of peak conductance was best fit to a single Boltzmann function and the voltage for half-maximal activation was –38.7 mV (Figure 3C).
evidence: Determined by voltage-clamp experiments and Boltzmann fitting shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The midpoint of the inactivation curve for sodium channels in proprioceptors is –64.5 mV.
source: The midpoint of the inactivation curve was –64.5 mV and was best fit to a single Boltzmann function (Figure 3D).
evidence: Determined by voltage-clamp experiments and Boltzmann fitting shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The tau for recovery from fast inactivation of sodium channels in proprioceptors is 0.54 ms.
source: INa recovery was rapid (τ = 0.54ms), with greater than 50% of INa recovered after 0.5 ms (Figure 3E).
evidence: Determined by voltage-clamp experiments with monoexponential fitting shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Greater than 50% of sodium current in proprioceptors recovers from fast inactivation after 0.5 ms.
source: INa recovery was rapid (τ = 0.54ms), with greater than 50% of INa recovered after 0.5 ms (Figure 3E).
evidence: Determined by voltage-clamp experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The tau for entry into slow inactivation of sodium channels in proprioceptors is 928.6 ms.
source: The tau for entry into slow inactivation was 928.6 ms, with more than 50% of channels available after a 2000 ms conditioning pulse.
evidence: Determined by voltage-clamp experiments with monoexponential fitting shown in Figure 3F.

claim: More than 50% of sodium channels in proprioceptors are available after a 2000 ms conditioning pulse at 0 mV.
source: The tau for entry into slow inactivation was 928.6 ms, with more than 50% of channels available after a 2000 ms conditioning pulse.
evidence: Determined by voltage-clamp experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: ICA 121431 application significantly reduces proprioceptor current density from ~–140 pA/pF to ~–75 pA/pF (p=0.0003).
source: Similar to serial pharmacological experiments, INa density in proprioceptors was significantly reduced from ~–140 pA/pF to ~–75 pA/pF following ICA application (Figure 4B, p=0.0003).
evidence: Determined by voltage-clamp experiments before and after ICA application shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ICA 121431 application significantly slows the proprioceptor sodium current tau from 0.6 ms to 1.0 ms (p=0.0007).
source: The proprioceptor INa had an average tau of 0.6 ms, which was significantly slowed to 1.0 ms following application of ICA (Figure 4C, p=0.0007), in line with loss of a fast gating channel.
evidence: Determined by voltage-clamp experiments before and after ICA application shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Blocking NaV1.1 does not change sodium current rise time in proprioceptors (p=0.1611).
source: Blocking NaV1.1 did not change INa rise time (Figure 4D, p=0.1611).
evidence: Determined by voltage-clamp experiments before and after ICA application shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The ICA-sensitive sodium current component in proprioceptors has an average tau of 0.4 ms.
source: Quantification of the ICA-sensitive component found an average tau of 0.4 ms and an average current density of –96 pA/pF (Figure 4E).
evidence: Determined by analyzing the ICA-sensitive current component shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The ICA-sensitive sodium current component in proprioceptors has an average current density of –96 pA/pF.
source: Quantification of the ICA-sensitive component found an average tau of 0.4 ms and an average current density of –96 pA/pF (Figure 4E).
evidence: Determined by analyzing the ICA-sensitive current component shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The ICA-sensitive current density in proprioceptors ranges from ~–28 pA/pF to ~–263 pA/pF.
source: Of note, there was a wide distribution of current densities for the ICA-sensitive component, ranging from ~–28 pA/pF to ~–263 pA/pF, suggesting some variability in the contribution of NaV1.1 to proprioceptor excitability that may be proprioceptor subtype dependent.
evidence: Observed from the distribution of ICA-sensitive current densities shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of NaV1.1 significantly reduces the number of evoked action potentials in most genetically identified proprioceptors.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of NaV1.1 significantly reduced the number of evoked action potentials in most genetically identified proprioceptors (Figure 4G); however, five of the cells recorded had low firing rates that were not inhibited by ICA.
evidence: Determined by current-clamp experiments before and after ICA application shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Five proprioceptor cells with low firing rates were not inhibited by ICA 121431.
source: Pharmacological inhibition of NaV1.1 significantly reduced the number of evoked action potentials in most genetically identified proprioceptors (Figure 4G); however, five of the cells recorded had low firing rates that were not inhibited by ICA.
evidence: Observed in current-clamp experiments shown in Figure 4G.

claim: ICA 121431 application significantly reduces action potential amplitude in proprioceptors (p=0.0420).
source: Action potential amplitude (Figure 4H, p=0.0420) and action potential threshold (Figure 4I, p=0.0186) were also significantly reduced following ICA application, and action potential full-width half-max was significantly increased following ICA application (Figure 4K, p=0.0068), in line with loss of the fast NaV1.1-mediated current.
evidence: Determined by current-clamp experiments before and after ICA application shown in Figure 4H.

claim: ICA 121431 application significantly reduces action potential threshold in proprioceptors (p=0.0186).
source: Action potential amplitude (Figure 4H, p=0.0420) and action potential threshold (Figure 4I, p=0.0186) were also significantly reduced following ICA application, and action potential full-width half-max was significantly increased following ICA application (Figure 4K, p=0.0068), in line with loss of the fast NaV1.1-mediated current.
evidence: Determined by current-clamp experiments before and after ICA application shown in Figure 4I.

claim: ICA 121431 application significantly increases action potential full-width half-max in proprioceptors (p=0.0068).
source: Action potential amplitude (Figure 4H, p=0.0420) and action potential threshold (Figure 4I, p=0.0186) were also significantly reduced following ICA application, and action potential full-width half-max was significantly increased following ICA application (Figure 4K, p=0.0068), in line with loss of the fast NaV1.1-mediated current.
evidence: Determined by current-clamp experiments before and after ICA application shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Scn1a-cKO mice display ataxic-like tremors when suspended in the air.
source: Consistent with in vitro data, Scn1a-cKO animals of both sexes displayed profound and visible motor abnormalities. These abnormalities include ataxic-like tremors when suspended in the air (Video 1), abnormal limb positioning (Videos 2 and 3), and paw clasping, which are absent in Scn1a-floxed littermate controls and heterozygous animals (PirtCre;Scn1afl/+, Scn1a-Het, respectively, Figure 5A).
evidence: Observed in behavioral analysis shown in Video 1 and Figure 5A.

claim: Scn1a-cKO mice display abnormal limb positioning.
source: Consistent with in vitro data, Scn1a-cKO animals of both sexes displayed profound and visible motor abnormalities. These abnormalities include ataxic-like tremors when suspended in the air (Video 1), abnormal limb positioning (Videos 2 and 3), and paw clasping, which are absent in Scn1a-floxed littermate controls and heterozygous animals (PirtCre;Scn1afl/+, Scn1a-Het, respectively, Figure 5A).
evidence: Observed in behavioral analysis shown in Videos 2 and 3 and Figure 5A.

claim: Scn1a-cKO mice display paw clasping.
source: Consistent with in vitro data, Scn1a-cKO animals of both sexes displayed profound and visible motor abnormalities. These abnormalities include ataxic-like tremors when suspended in the air (Video 1), abnormal limb positioning (Videos 2 and 3), and paw clasping, which are absent in Scn1a-floxed littermate controls and heterozygous animals (PirtCre;Scn1afl/+, Scn1a-Het, respectively, Figure 5A).
evidence: Observed in behavioral analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Scn1a-floxed littermate controls do not display ataxic-like tremors, abnormal limb positioning, or paw clasping.
source: These abnormalities include ataxic-like tremors when suspended in the air (Video 1), abnormal limb positioning (Videos 2 and 3), and paw clasping, which are absent in Scn1a-floxed littermate controls and heterozygous animals (PirtCre;Scn1afl/+, Scn1a-Het, respectively, Figure 5A).
evidence: Observed in behavioral analysis shown in Figure 5A and Videos 1-3.

claim: Scn1a-Het mice do not display ataxic-like tremors, abnormal limb positioning, or paw clasping.
source: These abnormalities include ataxic-like tremors when suspended in the air (Video 1), abnormal limb positioning (Videos 2 and 3), and paw clasping, which are absent in Scn1a-floxed littermate controls and heterozygous animals (PirtCre;Scn1afl/+, Scn1a-Het, respectively, Figure 5A).
evidence: Observed in behavioral analysis shown in Figure 5A and Videos 1-3.

claim: Scn1a-cKO animals traveled significantly less than Scn1a-floxed littermate controls in the open-field test (p=0.0077).
source: We found that Scn1a-cKO animals traveled significantly less (Figure 5C) and slower (Figure 5D) than Scn1a-floxed littermate controls (p=0.0077 and p=0.0057, respectively).
evidence: Determined by open-field behavioral testing shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Scn1a-cKO animals moved significantly slower than Scn1a-floxed littermate controls in the open-field test (p=0.0057).
source: We found that Scn1a-cKO animals traveled significantly less (Figure 5C) and slower (Figure 5D) than Scn1a-floxed littermate controls (p=0.0077 and p=0.0057, respectively).
evidence: Determined by open-field behavioral testing shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Scn1a-Het mice traveled significantly less than Scn1a-floxed littermate controls in the open-field test (p=0.0255).
source: Surprisingly, Scn1a-Het mice also displayed motor abnormalities in the open-field test, performing similarly to Scn1a-cKO animals (Figure 5B–D), demonstrating NaV1.1 haploinsufficiency in sensory neurons for motor behaviors.
evidence: Determined by open-field behavioral testing shown in Figure 5C with statistical analysis.

claim: Scn1a-Het mice moved significantly slower than Scn1a-floxed littermate controls in the open-field test (p=0.00311).
source: Surprisingly, Scn1a-Het mice also displayed motor abnormalities in the open-field test, performing similarly to Scn1a-cKO animals (Figure 5B–D), demonstrating NaV1.1 haploinsufficiency in sensory neurons for motor behaviors.
evidence: Determined by open-field behavioral testing shown in Figure 5D with statistical analysis.

claim: No genotype-dependent differences were observed in the amount of time spent moving in the open-field test.
source: No genotype-dependent differences were observed in the amount of time spent moving, suggesting gross motor function was intact (Figure 5E).
evidence: Determined by open-field behavioral testing shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The amount of time spent in the center of the open-field chamber was independent of genotype.
source: Additionally, the amount of time spent in the center of the open-field chamber was also independent of genotype (Figure 5F).
evidence: Determined by open-field behavioral testing shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Scn1a-floxed and Scn1a-Het mice performed at similar levels during the 3-day rotarod test.
source: Unlike in the open-field assay, both Scn1a-floxed and Scn1a-Het mice performed at similar levels during the 3-day period (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Determined by rotarod behavioral testing shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: Scn1a-cKO animals performed significantly worse than Scn1a-floxed and Scn1a-Het mice in the rotarod test.
source: Conversely, Scn1a-cKO animals performed significantly worse. By day 3, on average they were only able to maintain their position on the rotarod for 41 s, falling over 50% faster Scn1a-floxed and Scn1a-Het mice.
evidence: Determined by rotarod behavioral testing shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: By day 3 of rotarod testing, Scn1a-cKO animals maintained their position for an average of 41 seconds.
source: By day 3, on average they were only able to maintain their position on the rotarod for 41 s, falling over 50% faster Scn1a-floxed and Scn1a-Het mice.
evidence: Determined by rotarod behavioral testing shown in Figure 5H.

claim: No sex-dependent differences were observed in performance in the open-field test.
source: We did not observe any sex-dependent differences in performance in the open-field or rotarod tests (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Determined by analysis of sex-dependent parameters shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: No sex-dependent differences were observed in performance in the rotarod test.
source: We did not observe any sex-dependent differences in performance in the open-field or rotarod tests (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Determined by analysis of sex-dependent parameters shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Little-to-no neuronal expression of TdTomato was observed in dorsal and ventral spinal cord of PirtCre;Rosa26Ai14 mice.
source: We observed little-to-no neuronal expression of TdTomato in both dorsal and ventral spinal cord (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Determined by immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: DRG somata and axons showed strong TdTomato labeling in PirtCre;Rosa26Ai14 mice.
source: In contrast, DRG somata and axons showed strong labeling.
evidence: Observed in immunohistochemistry analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: No significant genotype-dependent differences were found in the number of Pvalb+/Runx3+ proprioceptors per DRG section between Scn1a-Het and Scn1a-cKO mice compared to Scn1a-floxed controls (p=0.3824 and p=0.1665, respectively).
source: We found no significant genotype-dependent differences in the number of proprioceptors in Scn1a-Het and Scn1a-cKO mice compared to Scn1a-floxed controls (p=0.3824 and p=0.1665, respectively), indicating that the behavioral deficits observed in Scn1a-cKO mice are not the result of a developmental loss of proprioceptors.
evidence: Determined by RNAscope analysis of DRG sections shown in Figure 6.

claim: No qualitative differences in muscle spindle morphology were observed between Scn1a-floxed, Scn1a-Het, and Scn1a-cKO genotypes.
source: We also analyzed muscle spindle morphology to determine whether aberrant sensory end organ development may contribute to the observed motor abnormalities. Similar to conditional Piezo2-knockout animals (Woo et al., 2015), no qualitative differences were observed between genotypes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Determined by analysis of muscle spindle whole mounts shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant decrease in VGLUT1 puncta density per ChAT+ neuron was found between Scn1a-Het or Scn1a-cKO compared to Scn1a-floxed littermate controls (Scn1a-Het, p>0.9999, Scn1a-cKO, p=0.4573).
source: We found no significant decrease in VGLUT puncta density per ChAT+ neuron between Scn1a-Het or Scn1a-cKO when compared to Scn1a-floxed littermate controls (Figure 7, Scn1a-Het, p>0.9999, Scn1a-cKO, p=0.4573).
evidence: Determined by immunohistochemistry analysis of spinal cord sections shown in Figure 7.

claim: Afferents from Scn1a-Het and Scn1a-cKO mice exhibited impaired static stretch sensitivity compared to Scn1a-floxed mice.
source: Afferents from both Scn1a-Het and Scn1a-cKO mice exhibited impaired static stretch sensitivity as evidenced by a decreased likelihood of firing during rest as compared to Scn1a-floxed mice, as well as an inability to maintain firing throughout the entire 4 s stretch.
evidence: Determined by ex vivo muscle afferent recordings shown in Figure 8.

claim: Almost all afferents from Scn1a-floxed mice could fire consistently throughout the entire 4 s hold phase of stretch.
source: Almost all afferents from Scn1a-floxed mice could fire consistently throughout the entire 4 s hold phase (Figure 8A), but loss of one or both copies of NaV1.1 led to either firing only near the beginning of stretch or inconsistent firing in a high percentage of afferents lacking NaV1.1 (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: Determined by ex vivo muscle afferent recordings shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Loss of one or both copies of NaV1.1 led to inconsistent firing in a high percentage of afferents during static stretch.
source: Almost all afferents from Scn1a-floxed mice could fire consistently throughout the entire 4 s hold phase (Figure 8A), but loss of one or both copies of NaV1.1 led to either firing only near the beginning of stretch or inconsistent firing in a high percentage of afferents lacking NaV1.1 (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: Determined by ex vivo muscle afferent recordings shown in Figure 8B and C.

claim: There is a significant effect of genotype on the coefficient of variation of interspike interval during the plateau phase of stretch (p=0.015).
source: We quantified this inconsistent firing by determining the CV of the interspike interval (ISI) during the plateau phase of stretch (1.5–3.5 s into the hold phase) across different stretch lengths and found a significant effect of genotype, with the knockout afferents both having higher ISI CV than the Scn1a-floxed afferents (Figure 8D; 0.074 ± 0.06, 0.313 ± 0.456, 0.497 ± 0.831, at 7.5% Lo, Scn1a-floxed, Scn1a-Het, and Scn1a-cKO afferents, respectively, two-way ANOVA, main effect of genotype, p=0.015).
evidence: Determined by ex vivo muscle afferent recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The ISI CV at 7.5% Lo is 0.074 ± 0.06 for Scn1a-floxed afferents, 0.313 ± 0.456 for Scn1a-Het afferents, and 0.497 ± 0.831 for Scn1a-cKO afferents.
source: We quantified this inconsistent firing by determining the CV of the interspike interval (ISI) during the plateau phase of stretch (1.5–3.5 s into the hold phase) across different stretch lengths and found a significant effect of genotype, with the knockout afferents both having higher ISI CV than the Scn1a-floxed afferents (Figure 8D; 0.074 ± 0.06, 0.313 ± 0.456, 0.497 ± 0.831, at 7.5% Lo, Scn1a-floxed, Scn1a-Het, and Scn1a-cKO afferents, respectively, two-way ANOVA, main effect of genotype, p=0.015).
evidence: Determined by ex vivo muscle afferent recordings shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Dynamic sensitivity was not significantly impaired in afferents lacking NaV1.1.
source: In contrast to the clear deficits in static sensitivity in afferents lacking NaV1.1, dynamic sensitivity was not significantly impaired.
evidence: Determined by ex vivo muscle afferent recordings shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The maximum firing frequency during the rampup phase (Dynamic Peak) was independent of genotype (p=0.0633).
source: The maximum firing frequency during the rampup phase (Dynamic Peak) was independent of genotype, and even trended slightly higher in afferents lacking NaV1.1 (Figure 8E; two-way ANOVA, effect of genotype p=0.0633).
evidence: Determined by ex vivo muscle afferent recordings with statistical analysis shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Afferents lacking NaV1.1 were equally likely to entrain to vibration as Scn1a-floxed afferents in most cases.
source: In most cases, afferents lacking NaV1.1 were equally likely to entrain to vibration than Scn1a-floxed afferents (Figure 9D–F).
evidence: Determined by ex vivo muscle afferent recordings during sinusoidal vibration shown in Figure 9D-F.

claim: Scn1a-cKO afferents were able to maintain firing during the entire 9 s sinusoidal vibration.
source: Indeed, Scn1a-cKO afferents were able to maintain firing during the entire 9 s sinusoidal vibration, in contrast to their inability to maintain consistent firing during 4 s of static stretch.
evidence: Determined by ex vivo muscle afferent recordings during sinusoidal vibration shown in Figure 9.

claim: There were no significant differences in firing rate during vibration between Scn1a-floxed, Scn1a-Het, and Scn1a-cKO afferents.
source: There were no significant differences in firing rate during vibration between Scn1a-floxed, Scn1a-Het, and Scn1a-cKO afferents (Figure 9D–F).
evidence: Determined by ex vivo muscle afferent recordings during sinusoidal vibration shown in Figure 9D-F.

claim: NaV1.1 is referred to as a 'super culprit' gene, with over 1000 associated mutations that lead to abnormal brain function.
source: Indeed, Scn1a, the gene that encodes NaV1.1, is referred to as a 'super culprit' gene, with over 1000 associated mutations that lead to abnormal brain function, resulting in brain disorders such as epilepsy and migraine, as well as neurodivergent phenotypes, such as autism spectrum disorder (Ding et al., 2021; Lossin, 2009).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Ding et al., 2021; Lossin, 2009).

claim: Homozygous Scn1a-/- global knockout mice are ataxic and die by postnatal day 15.
source: Homozygous Scn1a-/- global knockout mice are ataxic and die by postnatal day (P) 15, while heterozygous Scn1a+/- animals develop seizures and begin to die sporadically starting at P21 (Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Yu et al., 2006).

claim: Heterozygous Scn1a+/- global knockout mice develop seizures and begin to die sporadically starting at postnatal day 21.
source: Homozygous Scn1a-/- global knockout mice are ataxic and die by postnatal day (P) 15, while heterozygous Scn1a+/- animals develop seizures and begin to die sporadically starting at P21 (Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Yu et al., 2006).

claim: NaV1.1 is expressed in the peripheral nervous system.
source: In addition to the central nervous system (CNS), NaV1.1 is also expressed in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) (Sharma et al., 2020; Usoskin et al., 2015); yet, the prominent role this channel plays in brain function has left its physiological roles in sensory neuron populations understudied.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Sharma et al., 2020; Usoskin et al., 2015).

claim: Scn1a transcript and protein have been observed primarily in myelinated mechanosensory DRG and TG neurons.
source: Scn1a transcript and protein have been observed primarily in myelinated mechanosensory DRG and TG neurons (Fukuoka et al., 2008; Ho and O'Leary, 2011; Osteen et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Fukuoka et al., 2008; Ho and O'Leary, 2011; Osteen et al., 2016).

claim: Subcutaneous injection of the NaV1.1 activator, Hm1a, into mouse hind paw causes noninflammatory mechanical pain and spontaneous pain behaviors.
source: Indeed, subcutaneous injection of the NaV1.1 activator, Hm1a, into mouse hind paw causes noninflammatory mechanical pain and spontaneous pain behaviors (Osteen et al., 2016).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Osteen et al., 2016).

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of NaV1.1 does not affect mechanical thresholds in uninjured mice but does reduce mechanical pain in a spared-nerve injury model.
source: Interestingly, pharmacological inhibition of NaV1.1 does not affect mechanical thresholds in uninjured mice but does reduce mechanical pain in a spared-nerve injury model (Salvatierra et al., 2018), suggesting that NaV1.1 may have a more prominent role in mechanical pain as opposed to normal touch sensing.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Salvatierra et al., 2018).

claim: NaV1.1 in TG neurons mediates mechanical pain in an orbitofacial chronic constriction injury model.
source: NaV1.1 in TG neurons has also been reported to mediate mechanical pain in an orbitofacial chronic constriction injury model (Pineda-Farias et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Pineda-Farias et al., 2021).

claim: NaV1.1 is found in colon-innervating vagal neurons, where it contributes to firing of colonic mechano-nociceptors and is upregulated in a mouse model of chronic visceral hypersensitivity.
source: In addition to somatosensory neurons, NaV1.1 is found in colon-innervating vagal neurons, where it contributes to firing of colonic mechano-nociceptors and is upregulated in a mouse model of chronic visceral hypersensitivity (Osteen et al., 2016; Salvatierra et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Osteen et al., 2016; Salvatierra et al., 2018).

claim: NaV1.1 contributes to action potential firing in a subset of DRG neurons that express TRPM8.
source: Lastly, NaV1.1 contributes to action potential firing in a subset of DRG neurons that express the cold-sensitive ion channel, transient receptor potential melastatin 8 (TRPM8), suggesting that the channel may also contribute to thermosensory transmission (Griffith et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Griffith et al., 2019).

claim: RNA-sequencing datasets have consistently identified NaV1.1 expression in proprioceptors.
source: RNA-sequencing datasets have consistently identified NaV1.1 expression in proprioceptors; thus, we next analyzed NaV1.1 expression in these cells using a ParvalbuminCre;Rosa26Ai14 reporter line (PvalbAi14) and found that 100% of genetically identified proprioceptors were positive for Scn1a message (Figure 1B).
evidence: Referenced as established knowledge from RNA-sequencing datasets.

claim: NaV1.6 and NaV1.7 expression has been reported in proprioceptors.
source: In addition to NaV1.1, NaV1.6 and NaV1.7 expression has also been reported in proprioceptors (Carrasco et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Carrasco et al., 2017).

claim: NaV1.1 is haploinsufficient in several brain neuron cell types for normal excitability and function.
source: NaV1.1 is haploinsufficient in several brain neuron cell types for normal excitability and function (Ogiwara et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2006), suggesting the contributions of NaV1.1 to neuronal function are highly sensitive to genetic perturbations.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Ogiwara et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2006).

claim: Loss of a single copy of NaV1.1 is sufficient to attenuate sustained action potential firing in parvalbumin-positive hippocampal interneurons.
source: Indeed, loss of a single copy of NaV1.1 is sufficient to attenuate sustained action potential firing in parvalbumin-positive hippocampal interneurons (Ogiwara et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2006) and cerebellar Purkinje neurons (Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Ogiwara et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2006).

claim: Loss of a single copy of NaV1.1 is sufficient to attenuate sustained action potential firing in cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: Indeed, loss of a single copy of NaV1.1 is sufficient to attenuate sustained action potential firing in parvalbumin-positive hippocampal interneurons (Ogiwara et al., 2007; Yu et al., 2006) and cerebellar Purkinje neurons (Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Yu et al., 2006).

claim: NaV1.1 has been associated with persistent sodium current (INaP) and resurgent sodium current (INaR), both of which promote repetitive firing in a wide variety of cell types in the CNS and PNS.
source: NaV1.1 has been associated with persistent sodium current (INaP) and resurgent sodium current (INaR), both of which promote repetitive firing in a wide variety of cell types in the CNS and PNS (Barbosa et al., 2015; Kalume et al., 2007; Khaliq et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Barbosa et al., 2015; Kalume et al., 2007; Khaliq et al., 2003).

claim: NaV1.1 recovers rapidly from fast inactivation compared to other channel subtypes.
source: NaV1.1 also recovers rapidly from fast inactivation compared to other channel subtypes (Herzog et al., 2003; Patel et al., 2015) and has been shown to be refractory to entry into slow inactivation in TRPM8-expressing DRG neurons (Griffith et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Herzog et al., 2003; Patel et al., 2015).

claim: NaV1.1 has been shown to be refractory to entry into slow inactivation in TRPM8-expressing DRG neurons.
source: NaV1.1 also recovers rapidly from fast inactivation compared to other channel subtypes (Herzog et al., 2003; Patel et al., 2015) and has been shown to be refractory to entry into slow inactivation in TRPM8-expressing DRG neurons (Griffith et al., 2019).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Griffith et al., 2019).

claim: Loss of synaptic-like vesicle released glutamate from afferent endings produces a similar deficit in static but not dynamic sensitivity.
source: A similar deficit in static but not dynamic sensitivity was seen following loss of synaptic-like vesicle released glutamate from afferent endings (Than et al., 2021); however, in those afferents, firing only occurred at the beginning of stretch and patchy firing was never observed.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Than et al., 2021).

claim: Many epilepsy patients with hemizygous NaV1.1 loss of function display ataxia and motor delays and deficiencies.
source: Notably, Scn1a is a super culprit gene with over 1000 associated disease-causing mutations, most of which are linked to different forms of epilepsy. Many epilepsy patients with hemizygous NaV1.1 loss of function display ataxia and motor delays and deficiencies (Claes et al., 2001; Fujiwara et al., 2003), which has traditionally been attributed to loss of NaV1.1 function in the brain, namely, the cerebellum (Kalume et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Claes et al., 2001; Fujiwara et al., 2003).

claim: Motor deficits in epilepsy patients have traditionally been attributed to loss of NaV1.1 function in the brain, namely, the cerebellum.
source: Many epilepsy patients with hemizygous NaV1.1 loss of function display ataxia and motor delays and deficiencies (Claes et al., 2001; Fujiwara et al., 2003), which has traditionally been attributed to loss of NaV1.1 function in the brain, namely, the cerebellum (Kalume et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Kalume et al., 2007).

claim: NaV1.1 in proprioceptors is a dominant functional NaV subtype.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that in proprioceptors NaV1.1 is a dominant functional NaV subtype.
evidence: Inferred from serial pharmacological blockade experiments showing NaV1.1 comprises 44.8% of the whole-cell sodium current.

claim: NaV1.1 is required for transmission of receptor potentials generated during sustained muscle stretch.
source: This suggests that while a combination of Piezo2 and other NaV isoforms is sufficient to elicit activity in response to transient stimuli, NaV1.1 is required for transmission of receptor potentials generated during sustained muscle stretch.
evidence: Inferred from ex vivo recordings showing impaired static but not dynamic sensitivity in Scn1a-cKO afferents.

claim: NaV1.1 haploinsufficiency in sensory neurons impairs both proprioceptor function and motor behaviors.
source: Impressively, recordings from afferents of heterozygous conditional knockout animals were similarly impaired, and heterozygous conditional knockout mice also exhibited motor behavioral deficits. Thus, NaV1.1 haploinsufficiency in sensory neurons impairs both proprioceptor function and motor behaviors.
evidence: Supported by ex vivo recordings and behavioral data from Scn1a-Het mice.

claim: Sensory neuron dysfunction contributes to the clinical manifestations of neurological disorders in which NaV1.1 function is compromised.
source: Importantly, human patients harboring NaV1.1 loss-of-function mutations often present with motor delays and ataxia; therefore, our data suggest that sensory neuron dysfunction contributes to the clinical manifestations of neurological disorders in which NaV1.1 function is compromised.
evidence: Inferred from the findings in mouse models and known clinical presentations in human patients.

claim: NaV1.1 is essential for mammalian proprioceptive signaling and behaviors.
source: Collectively, we present the first evidence that NaV1.1 is essential for mammalian proprioceptive signaling and behaviors.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the combined data of expression analysis, electrophysiology, and behavioral experiments.

claim: Some proprioceptor subtypes rely more heavily on NaV1.6 and NaV1.7 for electrical activity.
source: In line with this, pharmacological inhibition of NaV1.1 is sufficient to significantly attenuate action potential firing in most proprioceptors; yet, it should be noted that 25% of the neurons we recorded fired action potentials that were insensitive to ICA application. This suggests that some proprioceptor subtypes rely more heavily on NaV1.6 and NaV1.7 for electrical activity.
evidence: Inferred from current-clamp experiments showing 25% of proprioceptors were insensitive to ICA.

claim: NaV1.1 has a specific role in proprioceptor responses to static muscle movement.
source: These results, however, should be interpreted with the caveat that in these experiments ICA may also be acting on NaV1.3 channels that are upregulated during DRG neuron culturing (Wangzhou et al., 2020). Nevertheless, at the afferent level Scn1a-cKO and Scn1a-Het animals show clear deficits in static stretch sensitivity, but not dynamic sensitivity, and could even entrain to vibrations as fast as 100 Hz, suggesting a specific role for NaV1.1 in proprioceptors responses to static muscle movement.
evidence: Inferred from ex vivo recordings showing impaired static but not dynamic sensitivity.

claim: The observed motor behavioral deficits in Scn1a-cKO mice are likely due to reduced static sensitivity of proprioceptor afferents.
source: Finally, we found that loss of NaV1.1 in sensory neurons had no effect on proprioceptor development, muscle spindle morphology, or proprioceptive afferent innervation of ChAT+ motor neurons in the spinal cord. Thus, the observed motor behavioral deficits are likely due to reduced static sensitivity of proprioceptor afferents.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of developmental deficits and the presence of functional deficits in static sensitivity.

claim: During dynamic or vibratory stimuli, Piezo2 and likely a combination of other molecular mediators, including NaV1.6 and NaV1.7, are sufficient to elicit normal electrical activity.
source: Our model proposes that NaV1.1 is tasked with maintaining consistent firing in spindle afferents during static muscle stretch for normal motor behaviors, whereby activation of the mechanotransduction channel Piezo2 initiates electrical signaling, which in turn activates a complement of TTX-sensitive NaV channels (Carrasco et al., 2017; Florez-Paz et al., 2016; Woo et al., 2015; Figure 10). During dynamic or vibratory stimuli, Piezo2, and likely a combination of other molecular mediators, including NaV1.6 and NaV1.7, are sufficient to elicit normal electrical activity.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings and cited literature (Carrasco et al., 2017; Florez-Paz et al., 2016; Woo et al., 2015).

claim: During prolonged muscle stretch when Piezo2 channels presumably inactivate, NaV1.1 is required for regular and reliable firing.
source: Conversely, during prolonged muscle stretch when Piezo2 channels presumably inactivate, NaV1.1 is required for regular and reliable firing.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings showing impaired static but not dynamic sensitivity.

claim: Vesicle-released glutamate contributes to mammalian proprioception.
source: While other signaling molecules and channels, such as vesicle-released glutamate (Bewick et al., 2005; Than et al., 2021), and mechanosensitive ASIC channels (Lin et al., 2016) and ENaC channels (Bewick and Banks, 2015), also contribute to mammalian proprioception, our data suggests that NaV1.1 is a critical for muscle spindle afferent mechanotransduction, given the overt behavioral deficits observed in Scn1a-cKO mice.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Bewick et al., 2005; Than et al., 2021).

claim: Mechanosensitive ASIC channels contribute to mammalian proprioception.
source: While other signaling molecules and channels, such as vesicle-released glutamate (Bewick et al., 2005; Than et al., 2021), and mechanosensitive ASIC channels (Lin et al., 2016) and ENaC channels (Bewick and Banks, 2015), also contribute to mammalian proprioception, our data suggests that NaV1.1 is a critical for muscle spindle afferent mechanotransduction, given the overt behavioral deficits observed in Scn1a-cKO mice.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Lin et al., 2016).

claim: ENaC channels contribute to mammalian proprioception.
source: While other signaling molecules and channels, such as vesicle-released glutamate (Bewick et al., 2005; Than et al., 2021), and mechanosensitive ASIC channels (Lin et al., 2016) and ENaC channels (Bewick and Banks, 2015), also contribute to mammalian proprioception, our data suggests that NaV1.1 is a critical for muscle spindle afferent mechanotransduction, given the overt behavioral deficits observed in Scn1a-cKO mice.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Bewick and Banks, 2015).

claim: NaV1.1 is critical for muscle spindle afferent mechanotransduction.
source: While other signaling molecules and channels, such as vesicle-released glutamate (Bewick et al., 2005; Than et al., 2021), and mechanosensitive ASIC channels (Lin et al., 2016) and ENaC channels (Bewick and Banks, 2015), also contribute to mammalian proprioception, our data suggests that NaV1.1 is a critical for muscle spindle afferent mechanotransduction, given the overt behavioral deficits observed in Scn1a-cKO mice.
evidence: Inferred from the overt behavioral deficits observed in Scn1a-cKO mice.

claim: Alterations in Golgi tendon organ function likely contribute to the behavioral deficits observed in Scn1a-cKO mice.
source: Due to the ubiquitous expression of NaV1.1 in all proprioceptors and the importance of Golgi tendon organ (GTO) feedback to motor control, alterations in function in those proprioceptors likely contribute to the behavioral deficits we observed; however, we did not directly measure their function.
evidence: Inferred from the ubiquitous expression of NaV1.1 in proprioceptors and the known importance of GTOs.

claim: ICA 121431 also blocks NaV1.3 channels.
source: It is important to note that ICA 121431 also blocks NaV1.3 channels, which could be upregulated in our cultured DRG neuron preparations (Wangzhou et al., 2020).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Wangzhou et al., 2020).

claim: A small but significant decrease in INa was observed in recordings from large-diameter DRG neurons harvested from Scn1a-cKO mice following ICA application (p=0.0041).
source: Indeed, a small but significant decrease in INa was observed in recordings from large-diameter DRG neurons harvested from PirtCre;Scn1a-floxed mice (Scn1a-cKO), which lack NaV1.1 in all sensory neurons. Thus, inhibition of upregulated NaV1.3 channels could contribute to the effect of on ICA on the proprioceptor INa(Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Determined by voltage-clamp experiments in Scn1a-cKO neurons shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of NaV1.1 in small- and medium-diameter DRG neurons using a peripherin-Cre driver did not produce visible motor deficits.
source: Deletion of NaV1.1 in small- and medium-diameter DRG neurons using a peripherin-Cre driver did not produce visible motor deficits (Osteen et al., 2016), indicating that sensory neuron populations in those categories are not involved.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Osteen et al., 2016).

claim: Baseline mechanical thresholds were unchanged following intraplantar injection of a selective NaV1.1 inhibitor.
source: Notably, baseline mechanical thresholds were unchanged following intraplantar injection of a selective NaV1.1 inhibitor (Salvatierra et al., 2018).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Salvatierra et al., 2018).

claim: Functional NaV1.1 protein may only be upregulated in tactile sensory neurons during pathological states.
source: This suggests that while NaV1.1 mRNA is expressed in most tactile sensory neurons, functional protein may only be upregulated in these populations during pathological states.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that NaV1.1 inhibition does not affect baseline mechanical thresholds.

claim: Loss of less than a quarter of the proprioceptor INa is sufficient to impair proprioceptor responsiveness to muscle stretch.
source: At the afferent level, heterozygous and homozygous loss of NaV1.1 produced similar deficits in static firing, suggesting that loss of less than a quarter of the proprioceptor INa is sufficient to impair proprioceptor responsiveness to muscle stretch.
evidence: Inferred from ex vivo recordings showing similar deficits in Scn1a-Het and Scn1a-cKO afferents.

claim: Loss of presynaptic NaV1.7 channels in the spinal cord reduced glutamate release from nociceptive afferents onto dorsal horn neurons.
source: For example, loss of presynaptic NaV1.7 channels in the spinal cord reduced glutamate release from nociceptive afferents onto dorsal horn neurons (MacDonald et al., 2021).
evidence: Cited from published literature (MacDonald et al., 2021).

claim: Some of the clinical manifestations associated with epilepsy may manifest in part as a result of unreliable coding by peripheral proprioceptors.
source: Notably, Scn1a is a super culprit gene with over 1000 associated disease-causing mutations, most of which are linked to different forms of epilepsy. Many epilepsy patients with hemizygous NaV1.1 loss of function display ataxia and motor delays and deficiencies (Claes et al., 2001; Fujiwara et al., 2003), which has traditionally been attributed to loss of NaV1.1 function in the brain, namely, the cerebellum (Kalume et al., 2007). Our findings suggest that some of the clinical manifestations associated with epilepsy are not solely due to NaV1.1 loss of function in the brain, but also may manifest in part as a result of unreliable coding by peripheral proprioceptors.
evidence: Inferred from the findings in mouse models showing proprioceptor dysfunction and motor deficits.

claim: There are anywhere from 5 to 8 different proprioceptor molecular subclasses.
source: There are anywhere from 5 to 8 different proprioceptor molecular subclasses (Oliver et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021), however, and it is possible that these distinct classes rely on different combinations of these channels for function.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Oliver et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021).

claim: Distinct proprioceptor subclasses may rely on different combinations of NaV channels for function.
source: There are anywhere from 5 to 8 different proprioceptor molecular subclasses (Oliver et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021), however, and it is possible that these distinct classes rely on different combinations of these channels for function.
evidence: Speculated based on the existence of multiple proprioceptor subclasses and observed variability in NaV expression.

claim: NaV1.1 may be localized to muscle spindle afferent endings where it helps amplify receptor current.
source: NaV1.1 has been localized to muscle spindle afferent endings and has been hypothesized to help amplify receptor current (Carrasco et al., 2017).
evidence: Cited from published literature (Carrasco et al., 2017).

claim: Amplification of the receptor potential by NaV1.1 is necessary to maintain firing during held stretch.
source: Our results support a model whereby current from Piezo2 and potentially other mechanically sensitive ion channels at the start of stretch produces a sufficient receptor potential to generate firing at the heminode, but that amplification of the receptor potential by NaV1.1 is necessary to maintain firing during held stretch.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings showing impaired static sensitivity in Scn1a-cKO afferents.

claim: Glutamate may play a more general role in maintaining excitability in proprioceptor afferents.
source: A similar deficit in static but not dynamic sensitivity was seen following loss of synaptic-like vesicle released glutamate from afferent endings (Than et al., 2021); however, in those afferents, firing only occurred at the beginning of stretch and patchy firing was never observed. This may indicate that glutamate plays a more general role maintaining excitability, whereas NaV1.1 is required for reliable action potential generation at heminodes during static stimuli.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with published findings (Than et al., 2021) and current results.

claim: NaV1.1 is required for reliable action potential generation at heminodes during static stimuli.
source: This may indicate that glutamate plays a more general role maintaining excitability, whereas NaV1.1 is required for reliable action potential generation at heminodes during static stimuli.
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings showing impaired static sensitivity in Scn1a-cKO afferents.

claim: NaV1.1 expressed along the axon could be essential for sustained static firing.
source: Alternatively, or in addition, NaV1.1 expressed along the axon could be essential for sustained static firing.
evidence: Speculated as an alternative mechanism for NaV1.1's role in static firing.

claim: The lack of an effect on dynamic sensitivity could suggest the upregulation of other NaV subtypes or other molecules as a compensatory mechanism to counteract the loss of NaV1.1.
source: The lack of an effect on dynamic sensitivity could suggest the upregulation of other NaV subtypes or other molecules as a compensatory mechanism to counteract the loss of NaV1.1.
evidence: Speculated as a possible explanation for the preserved dynamic sensitivity.

claim: Loss of proprioceptor activity does not generally reduce proprioceptive input into the spinal cord.
source: Additionally, we did not observe a general decrease in α-motor neuron innervation, which is consistent with the findings of Mendelsohn et al., 2015, who reported loss of proprioceptor activity does not generally reduce proprioceptive input into the spinal cord.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Mendelsohn et al., 2015).

claim: Loss of proprioceptor transmission causes changes in heteronymous sensory-motor connectivity, whereby proprioceptor innervation of motor neurons that project to antagonistic muscles is increased.
source: Interestingly, however, the authors did observe changes in heteronymous sensory-motor connectivity when proprioceptor transmission was blocked, whereby proprioceptor innervation of motor neurons that project to antagonistic muscles was increased.
evidence: Cited from published literature (Mendelsohn et al., 2015).

claim: Loss of NaV1.1 in proprioceptive afferents may cause them to 'mis-wire' and make connections with inappropriate motor neuron pools.
source: Whether loss of NaV1.1 in proprioceptive afferents causes them to 'mis-wire' in our model to make connections with inappropriate motor neuron pools is unclear.
evidence: Speculated as a possible mechanism contributing to behavioral deficits.
